USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current tariff posture and hold firm on existing demands without further escalation for now. The US has already imposed tariffs on roughly half of Chinese imports ($250 billion), and China has retaliated in kind. With the G20 truce just weeks old (Dec 1, 2018 ceasefire) and 90-day negotiations window open, the US should use this period to consolidate leverage and press for structural concessions rather than escalate further or concede.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate but manageable. The tariffs are causing sectoral pain—soybean prices down 20%, agricultural and auto exports hit hard by Chinese retaliation (Brookings, SCMP)—but the overall macroeconomic impact is described as 'a minor blip' for the US economy (Brookings). The US has structural leverage: China's export economy is more exposed, and the US has threatened to tariff the remaining ~$267 billion of Chinese imports if China retaliates further (Fox Business). However, the threat is not negligible—collateral damage to US firms operating in China, rising consumer prices from tariff pass-through (Fox Business explains tariffs are paid by US importers, not China), and disruption to global value chains where China is the final assembler but US firms capture profits (SCMP). The political environment favors holding firm: Trump sees this as a winning strategy post-midterms (Brookings), and the US has not yet exhausted its leverage. The risk of further escalation is that it could trigger a broader economic slowdown or market panic, but at current levels the US economy is absorbing the shock. The 90-day negotiation window agreed at G20 provides a natural pause to test whether China will offer meaningful structural reforms on IP theft, forced tech transfer, and market access—core US demands that go beyond purchase commitments.
key_factors: $250B in US tariffs already in place covering ~half of Chinese imports; $267B more threatened
China retaliation covers $110B of $130B US-China trade, nearly exhausting their tariff room
Soybean prices down 20%; agricultural/auto/Boeing sectors bearing concentrated pain
Tariffs paid by US importers, raising consumer prices domestically
Overall US economic impact described as 'minor blip' but sectoral damage real
China unlikely to 'cave' but willing to buy more and open markets
Collateral damage to US firms operating in China and global value chains

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should maintain its current retaliatory posture without further escalation, while signaling willingness to negotiate if the US demonstrates good faith. We should avoid making unilateral concessions that would embolden further US pressure, but also avoid provoking additional tariff rounds that would compound damage to our export economy.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is significant but not yet existential. The US has imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese goods (roughly half of bilateral trade), and Trump has threatened to tariff the remaining $267 billion if China retaliates further. China has already retaliated on $110 billion of the $130 billion in US imports available for targeting, meaning our retaliatory capacity is nearly exhausted. The Brookings analysis notes that while China is the final assembler, 'more than half of the value of those products are in parts and components from other countries,' meaning US tariffs also damage supply chains in ways that create leverage for China with third countries. However, the Washington Post reports that Chinese leaders feel betrayed after multiple failed deal attempts with Ross and Mnuchin that Trump personally vetoed, suggesting the US negotiating posture is unreliable. The Fox Business transcript confirms that 'almost all the cards have been played' on both sides. Given that our retaliatory tariff capacity is nearly maxed out and further escalation risks triggering the full $267 billion additional US tariffs, the prudent course is to hold current positions and wait for the post-midterm political environment to create space for genuine negotiations. China's offer to buy more US products and open markets remains on the table, which provides a face-saving off-ramp when talks resume.
key_factors: US tariffs cover $250B of ~$500B in Chinese exports to US, with threat to tariff remaining $267B
China has retaliated on $110B of $130B available US imports, nearly exhausting retaliatory capacity
More than half of value in Chinese exports comes from foreign components, limiting direct damage to China
Multiple failed US-China deal attempts (Ross deal, Mnuchin deal) vetoed by Trump suggest unreliable negotiating partner
Post-midterm political environment may create new negotiation window
China's soybean and agricultural retaliation hitting US Midwest politically but also hurting Chinese consumers
Soybean prices already down 20% per Brookings analysis
